Optical character recognition has a long history, and the problems it faces on a screen are not the problems it faces on a page. A scanned document arrives with paper texture, skew, and bleed-through from the reverse side. A screen region arrives clean, perfectly axis aligned, and free of noise, but it arrives at whatever size the display happened to render it.

That difference matters more than it first ap-

than any amount of clever thresholding.

Background polarity is the other common trap. A great deal of text on a modern desktop is light on a dark background, which is the inverse of every page the engine was trained on. Modern engines cope with this better than they once did, but making the input uniform costs almost nothing and removes a variable from every measurement taken downstream.
